title: Energy markets are being reshaped as supply chains endure testing times
gist: At a Gastech panel, energy leaders argued the Strait of Hormuz disruption shows markets adapting rather than splitting into strategic blocs, with countries choosing pragmatism over ideology (e.g., Germany restarting coal), and warned the market will not revert after Hormuz reopens because of lasting security fears.

insights.claim: The International Energy Forum's Secretary General argues energy markets are not ending but adapting to geopolitics, strategic competition and energy-security concerns, as shown by their response to Middle East disruptions.
insights.speaker: @energyconnects_
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the 'strategic bloc' fragmentation narrative; supports integrated global energy trade.
insights.quote: I don’t think the energy markets are ending
insights.locator: “I don’t think the energy markets are ending,”

insights.claim: Energy sector adaptability today reflects past investment decisions, so adequate and timely investment across all fuels and the supply chain is needed for resilience and future demand.
insights.speaker: @energyconnects_
insights.so_what: Underinvestment now means less flexibility in the next disruption; supports all-of-the-above energy capex.
insights.quote: Today’s energy sector adaptability is a reflection of yesterday’s investment decisions.

insights.claim: Market transparency on production levels, spare capacity, investment and infrastructure is essential to avoid 'informational choke points' that leave decision-makers without data.
insights.speaker: @energyconnects_
insights.so_what: Data opacity amplifies price spikes during supply shocks.
insights.quote: informational choke points where information is not available for decision-makers

insights.claim: Indo-Pacific countries are not aligning with either the US or China; the Strait of Hormuz crisis has pushed them to build resilience by switching fuels and dealing with friends and rivals to secure energy reserves.
insights.speaker: @energyconnects_
insights.so_what: Asian buyers will diversify suppliers opportunistically rather than along bloc lines.
insights.locator: On the geopolitical angle, Derek Grossman

insights.claim: In the last six months, ideologies that drove energy relationships have given way to practical national interest, exemplified by Germany restarting coal plants.
insights.speaker: @energyconnects_
insights.so_what: Energy-security pragmatism can extend demand for coal and other disfavored fuels.

insights.claim: The energy marketplace as known for 50 years has been completely scrambled, partly by electrification.
insights.speaker: @energyconnects_
insights.so_what: Structural regime change in energy trade patterns; historical relationships are less reliable guides.
insights.quote: the energy marketplace, as we have known it for 50 years, has been completely scrambled
insights.locator: “It’s not that the energy market has ended

insights.claim: The East Mediterranean Gas Forum sees energy as a possible prelude to political alignment by pairing stranded resources with countries that have markets or infrastructure.
insights.speaker: @energyconnects_
insights.so_what: Regional gas cooperation could unlock stranded East Med resources.
insights.quote: Maybe we can have energy as some sort of a prelude to political alignment and mutual interests in energy.
insights.locator: “Maybe for the first time we can see

insights.claim: Energy markets will not return to their prior state after the Strait of Hormuz reopens because buyers fear a repeat disruption.
insights.speaker: @energyconnects_
insights.so_what: Expect durable diversification, storage and security-premium spending beyond the crisis.
insights.quote: I don’t think we’re going back to the same thing after Hormuz reopens because people are scared it can happen again.

insights.claim: Energy security equals food security, especially for countries with large, poor populations.
insights.speaker: @energyconnects_
insights.so_what: Energy shocks transmit to food inflation and political risk in populous emerging markets.
